_about: The prayer hub (plan 7.6f), built the way love and righteousness are: the rows are defined by the Hebrew and Greek, a verb row by who prays and what the verb's own clause names (frames and clauses), a noun row by the words standing in the noun's phrase or verse, and a verse sits in every row it fits (match: all). Prayer leads with the verb: the text mostly says who prayed, to whom and for what. The review panel flagged prayer low (committee-flags.json): prayer to the saints and the Virgin, set prayers and liturgy and prayer in tongues are not in the grouping, and פָּלַל also means 'intercede, judge'. So: no row on any practice that is not in the text; the rows are by who prays and to whom as the verses read; each word counts only where its verse renders it as prayer; and what the text says of Christ's and the Spirit's intercession, of 'the Lord' as the one prayed to, and of the prayers of the saints is set out as written, with a note that the page takes no side. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/prayer.json.

titles.verb: Who prays, to whom, and for what
titles.noun: What the text says of prayer

_words_why: The card's own words are προσεύχομαι and προσευχή, פָּלַל and תְּפִלָּה, and the Aramaic בָּעוּ. Added as the same act in other words of the same languages: δέομαι and its noun δέησις (the Greek Old Testament renders the Hebrew supplication nouns תְּחִנָּה and תַּחֲנוּן by δέησις), the Hebrew verb עָתַר ('pray, entreat', Exod 8-10), the Aramaic verbs צלה and בעה (Dan 6; Ezra 6:10), ἐντυγχάνω / ὑπερεντυγχάνω ('intercede', Rom 8; Heb 7:25) and εὐχή in the one verse where it is 'prayer' (Jas 5:15). Each counts ONLY where its verse renders it as prayer, petition, supplication or intercession (the 'sense' below): δέομαι is 'beg, ask' of people as often as of God (Luke 8:28, Acts 21:39, 2 Cor 5:20 are not prayer) and counts in 7 of its 22 verses; פָּלַל also means 'intercede, judge' (Ezek 16:52) and counts in 79 of its 82; בעה is 'ask, seek' in nine of twelve verses; תְּחִנָּה is 'grace, mercy' in Ezra 9:8 and Josh 11:20. Different words the English also renders 'pray' or 'intercede' (εὔχομαι, פָּגַע, חָנַן and the rest) are named apart, in 'others'.
_sense_why: The Berean's wording: pray, prayer, petition, supplication, intercede, entreat, plea. '^(?!I pray$)' leaves out Acts 8:34, where δέομαι is glossed 'I pray' in the old sense of 'I beg you' and the eunuch is asking Philip ('Tell me, who is the prophet talking about?'). 'plea' is תְּחִנָּה in Solomon's prayer (1 Kgs 8; 2 Chr 6) and Jeremiah; 'pleaded' is not counted (Acts 25:24 is a petition to Festus).

sense_keep.Luke.22.32: Berean: 'But I have prayed for you, Simon' (MACULA glosses δέομαι 'begged')
sense_keep.1Thess.3.10: Berean: 'Night and day we pray most earnestly' (δέομαι glossed 'imploring')
sense_keep.Matt.9.38: Berean: 'Ask the Lord of the harvest' -- the same saying as Luke 10:2, where it is 'pray earnestly to', and a request made of God (δέομαι glossed 'Beseech')
sense_keep.Rom.11.2: Berean: 'how he appealed to God against Israel' -- ἐντυγχάνω with 'to God' (glossed 'he pleads')

_panel: Panel 2026-10-10 (hubs/prayer-panel.json): 'ship after fixes', 12 fixes. Taken: Matt 19:13 to 'Asked to pray for them'; 'Praying to the LORD, to God' and 'Praying for others' (tense), the Jeremiah prohibitions out of the latter; 'The Spirit intercedes; Christ intercedes'; the incense, Spirit and 'to be seen' labels and notes; Zech 12:10 first and its Hebrew; the confession and healing notes (Israel's prayers first; Jas 5:15 added, so healing is by pick); 'Prayer not heard, shut out, hindered' and 'Prayer and believing' as new rows; Neh 1:11 and 1 Kgs 8:52 out of 'Prayer and petition'; the verb catch-all note (Isa 45:14, idols, a king); John 17 as ἐρωτάω in others. The two fasting rows were cut to keep the count down. Left for Doug: Acts 7:59-60 ('Lord Jesus, receive my spirit', ἐπικαλέομαι) as prayer addressed to Jesus by name.
_review: Before the panel. Its flag (committee-flags.json, low): prayer to saints and the Virgin, set prayers and liturgy, and prayer in tongues are not in the grouping but a reader may look for them; פָּלַל is not only prayer. Taken so: no row on any practice that is not in the text; the rows are by who prays and to whom as the verses read; פָּלַל counts only where its verse renders it as prayer (3 of 82 do not); the verses that bear on intercession by the living (asked to pray for them), by Christ and the Spirit (He intercedes for us), and on 'the prayers of the saints' (prayer rises before God) are each set out as written with a note that the page takes no side; 'the Lord' prayed to (Acts 1:24; 8:22, 24) is its own row, unresolved. 1 Cor 14:14-15 (praying 'in a tongue', 'with my spirit') sits in 'Prayer and the Spirit' as the text has it, with no row on tongues as a practice.

others._why: Words the English renders as prayer, petition, supplication or intercession that are not this concept's own words (as love names φιλέω and חֶסֶד apart): named apart with their verses and never handed over as the same. Among them פָּגַע 'intercede' (Isa 53:12; Jer 7:16; 27:18) is the Hebrew behind the intercession of the Servant, and εὔχομαι the verb of 'we pray that you do no wrong' (2 Cor 13:7).
others.title: Other words translated “pray”, “petition”, “intercede”

g2065.note: John 17 is Jesus' own prayer: He lifts His eyes to heaven and says “Father” (17:1). The Greek word in these three is ἐρωτάω, “ask”, not προσεύχομαι; it is named here, apart, and the page does not hand one word over as the other.

rows.label: Jesus prays
rows.note: Where a verse says only “He”, the verses just before name Jesus. Luke 22:43-44 is absent from some early manuscripts.
rows._why: by hand, as the divine persons are: the verses where the Greek's agent is Jesus (frames) and the Berean's verse shows him praying -- by name (Mark 1:35, Luke 6:12, 9:18, 11:1, Heb 5:7) or as the one whose prayer in the garden is told ('My Father', Matt 26:39) or who says 'I have prayed for you' (Luke 22:32)

rows.label: Prayer to the Father
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the text itself names the Father ('your Father', 'Our Father', 'My Father') in the prayer

rows.label: Prayer to “the Lord”
rows.note: The text says “the Lord”; readers take it of the Father or of Jesus, and the page does not choose.

rows.label: Praying to the LORD, to God

not_verses.Rom.8.27: God is named as the measure ('according to the will of God'), not the one prayed to -- and the Spirit's intercession has its own row
not_verses.Phil.1.9: 'this is my prayer' names no one prayed to; 'God' stands in the clause of the glory the fruit is to bring
not_verses.Col.4.3: God is the one who may open a door, not named as the one prayed to
not_verses.1Sam.2.25: the LORD is the one sinned against, and no one is said to be prayed to
not_verses.2Sam.21.14: 'God heeded the supplications for the land' tells an answer, not a prayer made to Him
not_verses.2Sam.24.25: 'the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land' tells an answer, not a prayer made to Him

rows.label: Praying for others, on their behalf

not_verses.Jer.7.16: forbidden, not done: its own row, “Do not pray for this people”
not_verses.Jer.11.14: forbidden, not done: its own row, “Do not pray for this people”
not_verses.Jer.14.11: forbidden, not done: its own row, “Do not pray for this people”
not_verses.Rom.8.27: the Spirit's intercession, its own row; the page does not set it beside human prayer
not_verses.Rom.8.34: Christ's intercession, its own row; the page does not set it beside human prayer
not_verses.Heb.7.25: Christ's intercession, its own row; the page does not set it beside human prayer

rows.label: Asked to pray for them
rows.note: Each is a person in the text asking another person to pray for him or for them.
rows._why: by hand: the rule 'told to pray' (below) cannot tell a request for another's prayers from a command

rows.label: Told to pray

not_verses.Jer.7.16: forbidden, not commanded: its own row, below
not_verses.Jer.11.14: forbidden, not commanded: its own row, below
not_verses.Jer.14.11: forbidden, not commanded: its own row, below

rows.note: An imperative, whoever speaks it: Jesus to his disciples (“Pray that ...”), the apostles to the churches, Pharaoh to Moses (“Pray to the LORD”). A verse that is also a request for another's prayer stands in that row too.

rows.label: The Spirit intercedes; Christ intercedes
rows.note: The text says the Spirit intercedes (Rom 8:26-27) and that Christ does (Rom 8:34; Heb 7:25). What this intercession is, the page does not say.

rows.label: Prayer and the Spirit, or the spirit
rows.note: The verses that set prayer and the Spirit or the spirit together, as written. In Zech 12:10 the Hebrew is “a spirit of grace and supplications”, poured out by God. Where readers part on what praying in the Spirit is, or whose “spirit” prays in 1 Cor 14:14, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Praying to be seen; “babbling” like the pagans
rows.note: These are Jesus' words about prayer meant to be seen and prayer thought to work by its length; the page draws no conclusion about set or lengthy prayer.
rows._why: by hand: the four verses that name a prayer made to be seen or heard (“they love to pray standing in the synagogues”, “do not babble on like pagans”, “for a show make lengthy prayers”); a rule on the verb would take every prayer

rows.label: Prayer toward this house, this place, this city
rows._why: by hand: Solomon's prayer at the dedication, told twice (1 Kgs 8; 2 Chr 6), its refrain 'when they pray toward this place', and the two verses that do the same (Jonah 2:7; Dan 6:10 'the windows ... opened toward Jerusalem')

rows.label: Prayer, confession and forgiveness

not_verses.Matt.26.44: ἀφίημι here is 'left' (“He left them and went away once more”), not forgive

rows.note: Set out as the verses have them: Israel's own prayers of confession (1 Kgs 8; 2 Chr 6-7; Neh 1; Dan 9) first, then the New Testament verses. Where Christian traditions part on confession, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Prayer and healing
rows.note: Set out as the verses have them: prayer, and healing named in the same verse. In Gen 20:17 it is the barrenness of Abimelech's household that is healed; in 2 Chr 7:14, the land; in Isa 19:22, Egypt. Where Christian traditions part on healing and anointing (Jas 5:14-16), the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand (panel): the rule on the verb could not reach Jas 5:15 ('the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick'), whose prayer word is the noun εὐχή, so the passage was cut in the middle; the Hebrew verses are listed first

rows.label: Every other use: prays, prayed
rows.note: Includes prayer to idols (Isa 44:17; 45:20), prayer at a foreign sanctuary (Isa 16:12) and petition to a king (Dan 6:7, 6:12), where the same verbs are used, and Isa 45:14, where the Hebrew verb is the verb for praying (“they will make supplication to you”, said of the nations and Zion) though the Berean prints “confess”.

rows.label: A house of prayer, a place of prayer
rows._add_why: 'a place of prayer' (τόπος προσευχῆς / προσευχή as the place, Acts 16:13, 16:16): the noun stands alone, with no 'house'

rows.label: “A prayer of David”: prayers named for who prayed them
rows._why: by hand: the verses that call a psalm or a song a prayer, and say whose (David, Moses, 'one who is afflicted', Habakkuk)

rows.label: Prayer and petition

not_verses.Neh.1.11: תְּפִלָּה twice and no petition word: the verse shows one of the two words
not_verses.1Kgs.8.52: תְּחִנָּה twice and no prayer word: the verse shows one of the two words

rows.note: The text sets these two words side by side: תְּפִלָּה with תְּחִנָּה or תַּחֲנוּן, προσευχή with δέησις.

not_verses.Isa.37.4: the LORD hears the words of the Rabshakeh; 'prayer' is Hezekiah's call to lift up another
not_verses.2Kgs.19.4: the LORD hears the words of the Rabshakeh; 'prayer' is Hezekiah's call to lift up another
not_verses.Prov.18.23: 'answers' is the rich man answering the poor man, not the LORD answering prayer
not_verses.Jer.37.20: the king is asked to listen to a petition, not the LORD
not_verses.Prov.28.9: the 'hearing' is of the law, not of the prayer
not_verses.Isa.1.15: “I will not listen”: stands in “Prayer not heard, shut out”
not_verses.Jer.7.16: “I will not listen to you”: stands in “Prayer not heard, shut out”
not_verses.Jer.11.14: “I will not be listening”: stands in “Prayer not heard, shut out”
not_verses.Ps.35.13: “my prayers returned unanswered”: stands in “Prayer not heard, shut out”

rows.label: Prayer not heard, shut out, hindered
rows._why: by hand (panel): the verses that say prayer is refused, shut out, unanswered or hindered ('I will not listen', 'my prayers returned unanswered', 'He shuts out my prayer', 'no prayer can pass through', 'even his prayer is detestable', 'so that nothing will hinder your prayers'); they had been softened into 'Hearing and answering prayer'

rows.label: Prayer and believing
rows.note: The verses that name believing or faith as the prayer is made: whatever is asked in prayer, believing (Matt 21:22; Mark 11:24); “the prayer offered in faith” (Jas 5:15). Set out as written; the page takes no side on how faith and prayer relate.
rows._why: by hand (panel): a rule on πίστις / πιστεύω would also take Luke 22:32, 1 Thess 3:10 and Acts 14:23, where faith is not how the prayer is made

rows.label: The prayer of the righteous, of the wicked

not_verses.Jer.31.9: יָשָׁר is a 'level' path here, not an upright man
not_verses.Ps.141.5: the righteous man strikes and rebukes the speaker; the verse is not about whose prayer is heard

rows.label: Prayer goes up to God; prayers and incense
rows.note: The text's own picture, kept as written. Incense is in Ps 141:2 and Rev 5:8, 8:3-4; in Rev 5:8 the bowls are before the Lamb. In Rev 5:8 and 8:3-4 it is “the prayers of the saints”; what that shows about the saints and the angels, readers part on, and the page takes no side.

rows.label: Prayer with thanks, and “remembering you in my prayers”
Devoted to prayer, night and day
rows._add_why: 'I now pray before You day and night' -- the Hebrew has the pair, which the rule reads only in the Greek

rows.label: Every other use: prayer, petition
rows.note: Includes petitions made to a man, where the same Hebrew words are not prayer to God: תְּחִנָּה to the king (Jer 37:20; 38:26), תַּחֲנוּן of the poor man and of Leviathan (Prov 18:23; Job 41:3).
